llm_major: The first consensus claim says ML detects anomalous journal entries and fraudulent statements with 'promising performance', but 10.1109/access.2022.3153478 has no visible results and 10.4192/1577-8517-v11_4 reports no validation or accuracy. 10.2308/ajpt-50009 and the reviews concern firm-level fraud prediction, so only 10.3390/systems10050130 addresses journal entries, and only for predefined anomalies.

rq4 asks about mechanisms and conditions (skepticism, client complexity, firm size, regulation), but only one archival study (10.1108/maj-03-2023-3846, effort lag) supplies a mechanism. 10.13189/ujaf.2021.090527 is truncated and about internal auditors, and 10.1111/1911-3846.12894 and 10.1111/1911-3846.12901 do not test client complexity, firm size, or regulation.
llm_minor: The conditional claim says efficiency benefits appear 'only when auditor and client use AI jointly', but 10.1007/s11142-022-09697-x finds lower fees from audit-firm AI investment alone. The joint-use condition holds only for report lag in 10.1108/maj-03-2023-3846.

The conflict's side B uses internal-audit function size (10.1111/1911-3846.12847) as evidence that AI slows audits or raises costs, yet that same paper finds fewer audit days. This is a different setting and outcome, so the conflict is partly constructed.

rq5 names false positives, explainability, data quality, and liability, but no cited paper addresses these. The rq5 consensus covers only adoption lag, ethical/privacy concerns, and technology readiness.
The AI-cost gap proposes PCAOB Form AP as a source of audit hours, but Form AP does not disclose engagement hours, so the proposed design cannot be executed with that data.
actions: synthesize: split the rq3 claim into firm-level financial-statement fraud prediction and transaction/journal-entry anomaly detection. Cite only papers with reported results for 'performance', state that journal-entry evidence is a single predefined-anomaly experiment, and note that 10.4192/1577-8517-v11_4 and 10.1109/access.2022.3153478 do not support accuracy claims. Also search rq3: empirical studies reporting precision/recall for journal-entry or transaction-level anomaly detection in audit data.

search rq4: empirical studies (archival, experimental, or field) on how auditor AI/analytics affects professional skepticism and judgment, and moderation by client complexity, audit firm size (Big 4 vs non-Big 4), or regulatory regime

rationale: Only rq4 is flagged for search, so I added three queries aimed at the critic's gaps: experimental evidence on skepticism and judgment, firm-size moderation, and client-complexity moderation. The rq3 and rq5 search suggestions and the synthesis fixes are not flagged, so they are left to the synthesis redo.

llm_major: rq3 asks about accuracy on fraudulent transactions and journal entries, but the only comparative accuracy result (10.2308/ajpt-50009, 2011) is firm-level financial-statement fraud prediction with conventional models, and the one journal-entry paper (10.3390/systems10050130) tests predefined anomalies on a single ledger. The insurance-claims paper reports no validation, the access.2022.3153478 paper shows no results, and the two reviews are not audit-specific, so the question is effectively unanswered.
llm_minor: The rq3 'consensus' rests on one comparative study (10.2308/ajpt-50009) plus two reviews that add no accuracy findings, so it is a single-study result rather than a cross-paper consensus. It also concerns firm-level fraud prediction, not transaction or journal-entry detection.

The efficiency claim treats lower audit fees (10.1007/s11142-022-09697-x, 0.9% per SD) and report lag as evidence of efficiency, although fees are a price and not audit hours or effort. The perception surveys (10.15611/pn.2022.4.06) and internal-audit evidence are weak support, and no external-audit hours evidence exists.

Conflict 1 compares the report-lag result of 10.1108/maj-03-2023-3846 on both sides and sets it against the fee result in 10.1007/s11142-022-09697-x, which is a different outcome. Side B's 'audit-firm AI alone is linked to efficiency gains' is not supported by a lag finding. Conflict 2 contrasts firm-level AI investment with partner expertise premiums, which are different constructs, so it is closer to a distinction than a contradiction.

The claim that studies 'agree that analytics can undermine auditor judgment' cites 10.1111/1911-3846.12894, which shows reviewers rate D&A procedures as lower quality. That is reviewer perception, not auditor judgment. The remaining support is a reli-2 narrative review (10.5117/mab.96.78525) and interviews, and none concerns AI anomaly detection directly.

The conditional section includes the journal-entry and insurance-claims item (10.3390/systems10050130, 10.4192/1577-8517-v11_4), which states a limitation and names no moderator. The fee-premium item is a moderator of partner expertise pricing, not of AI's effect on audit outcomes.

No paper tests the named moderators (client complexity, firm size, regulation) or auditor use of AI flags. The evidence is generic D&A experiments, interviews, and one archival effort-lag mechanism (10.1108/maj-03-2023-3846).

The coverage note says the searches on false positives, explainability, data quality, liability and PCAOB/IAASB guidance were never run. The rq5 risk dimension therefore rests on descriptive ethics and tool reviews (10.1108/aaaj-09-2020-4934, 10.17261/pressacademia.2020.1337).

rq1 covers misstatement and fraud detection and discretionary accruals, but the evidence is restatement likelihood only. A lower restatement rate could mean fewer errors or less detection, and the Nigerian survey (10.22624/aims/humanities/v11n1p4) uses perceived quality.
actions: search rq3: empirical studies of ML or unsupervised anomaly detection on real or labelled journal-entry or transaction data in audit settings, reporting precision/recall or false-positive rates, e.g. on AAER-labelled or confirmed-misstatement cases

rationale: Only rq3 is flagged for new search; the other critic items concern synthesis or sub-questions not flagged, and rq4 already received new queries earlier. The new rq3 queries target labelled or real journal-entry and transaction data with reported precision, recall and false-positive rates, using different vocabulary from the earlier queries.

llm_major: rq3 asks about accuracy at identifying fraudulent transactions and journal entries in audit settings. The only audit-relevant papers are 10.3390/systems10050130 (one ledger, predefined anomalies), 10.4192/1577-8517-v11_4 (no validation) and 10.1109/access.2022.3153478 (no results shown). The rest are firm-level or non-audit fraud models, so it is effectively unanswered despite passing the count.
llm_minor: rq1 is supported only by restatement likelihood (10.1007/s11142-022-09697-x, 10.1108/maj-03-2023-3846) and a perception survey (10.22624/aims/humanities/v11n1p4). No paper covers misstatement or fraud detection or discretionary accruals, and 10.1108/ara-03-2024-0085 concerns client AI use.

The rq4 mechanism and moderator evidence consists of generic audit data analytics work (10.1111/1911-3846.12894, 10.5117/mab.96.78525, 10.1111/1911-3846.12901) plus one effort-lag mediation in 10.1108/maj-03-2023-3846. Client complexity, firm size and regulation are untested, and no paper examines how auditors act on AI flags.

The coverage_note field is corrupted by stray text ('}</br>Correction: the JSON above must be a single object; see below.</br>{'). It also claims the critic's requested searches are still outstanding, which is stale process commentary rather than evidence coverage.

The fee results are not in the rq2 consensus. They point in opposite directions: 10.1007/s11142-022-09697-x reports lower fees with firm AI investment, while 10.1080/09638180.2023.2298433 reports a fee premium for digitally expert partners. The synthesis lists no conflict and mentions this only in the coverage note.

The risk gap proposes a survey and interviews, but its stated outcome (the share of AI output accepted as sufficient evidence) cannot be obtained from document analysis, so the design does not fit the gap on explainability, data quality and liability.

The quality gap instruments AI investment with the firm's pre-period digital hiring, which is likely correlated with firm quality and client selection. The exclusion restriction is not defended, so the proposed identification is weak.
